REHAB26-ViewAngles: data pipeline, baseline, and first experiments¶

Capstone Part 2. This notebook builds the data pipeline, trains a baseline MLP and a first 1D CNN, and runs two sets of experiments that each change one factor: the feature representation (model held fixed) and the model (features held fixed).

Task: given the pose sequence of one exercise repetition from one camera, predict whether it was performed correctly (0) or incorrectly (1).

Data: Jánošová, Budikova, & Sedmidubsky (2026), https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23018128.

1. Setup¶

In [1]:

TEST_PERSON = "Vasil"  # held out entirely; not used anywhere in this notebook
SEEDS = (0, 1, 2)
EPOCHS = 30
BATCH = 64
LR = 1e-3
WEIGHT_DECAY = 1e-2

2. Data pipeline¶

2.1 Load labels and slice repetitions¶

Segmentation.csv gives the first and last frame of every labeled repetition. Each repetition was recorded by three synchronized cameras, and each camera has its own MediaPipe pose array of shape (frames, 33, 4) (x, y, z in metres centred on the hips, plus a visibility score). One sample is one repetition seen from one camera.

Repetitions last between 1.1 and 7.5 seconds, and incorrect ones are longer on average. Every repetition is therefore linearly resampled to a fixed 64 frames. This makes batching straightforward and removes duration as a shortcut to the label.

In [2]:
seg = pd.read_csv(DATA / "raw/Segmentation.csv", sep=";")
seg["y"] = (seg.correctness_score == 5).astype(int)          # 1 = incorrect, 0 = correct
seg["error"] = seg.error_description.fillna("correct")
seg["n_frames"] = seg.last_frame - seg.first_frame + 1
seg["rep_id"] = np.arange(len(seg))
EX_NAME = {1: "Arm abduction", 6: "Squat", 7: "Shoulder extension"}
EX_INDEX = {1: 0, 6: 1, 7: 2}
CAM_ANGLE = {1: 0, 2: 45, 3: 90}     # approximate camera positions around the participant (degrees)


def resample(seq, n):
    # Linear interpolation of a (frames, ...) array to n evenly spaced time steps.
    pos = np.linspace(0, len(seq) - 1, n)
    lo = np.floor(pos).astype(int)
    hi = np.minimum(lo + 1, len(seq) - 1)
    w = (pos - lo).reshape(-1, *[1] * (seq.ndim - 1))
    return seq[lo] * (1 - w) + seq[hi] * w


X, rows = [], []
for (vid, ex), reps in seg.groupby(["video_id", "exercise_id"]):
    for cam in (1, 2, 3):
        arr = np.load(DATA / f"mediapipe/ex{ex}/{vid}_cam{cam}_3d.npy")
        for r in reps.itertuples():
            clip = arr[r.first_frame:r.last_frame + 1]
            assert len(clip) == r.n_frames and np.abs(clip[:, :, :3]).sum(axis=(1, 2)).min() > 0
            X.append(resample(clip, T))
            rows.append(dict(rep_id=r.rep_id, person=r.person, exercise_id=ex, exercise=EX_NAME[ex], cam=cam,
                             orientation=r.person_orientation, view=CAM_ANGLE[cam] - r.person_orientation,
                             y=r.y, error=r.error, n_frames=r.n_frames))
X = np.stack(X).astype(np.float32)
meta = pd.DataFrame(rows)
P = X[..., :3]                       # joint positions, (N, T, 33, 3)
N = len(meta)
print("Pose tensor:", X.shape, "| repetitions:", meta.rep_id.nunique(), "| sequences:", N)
print("Class balance:", meta.y.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict(), "(0 = correct, 1 = incorrect)")

Pose tensor: (4995, 64, 33, 4) | repetitions: 1665 | sequences: 4995
Class balance: {0: 2496, 1: 2499} (0 = correct, 1 = incorrect)

2.2 Why coordinates need more than scaling¶

The 3D landmarks are centred on the hips, but their axes follow the camera. As the participant turns from 0° to 90°, the whole skeleton rotates in the coordinate system, and it also differs between the three cameras. The plot below shows the direction of the shoulder line seen from above for every sequence.

To give coordinates a fair comparison against joint angles, I add a feature set where each repetition is rotated about the vertical axis so that the participant faces the same way. The rotation is estimated once per repetition from the starting pose, so genuine torso rotation during the movement is preserved.

In [3]:
L_SH, R_SH, L_HIP, R_HIP = 11, 12, 23, 24


def torso_length(P):
    mid_sh = (P[:, :, L_SH] + P[:, :, R_SH]) / 2
    mid_hip = (P[:, :, L_HIP] + P[:, :, R_HIP]) / 2
    return np.linalg.norm(mid_sh - mid_hip, axis=-1).mean(axis=1)        # (N,)


def scale_normalize(P):
    # Divide by the repetition's mean torso length so body size does not matter.
    return P / torso_length(P)[:, None, None, None]


def canonicalize_rotation(P, start_frac=0.1):
    # Rotate each repetition about the vertical (y) axis so the starting pose faces the camera.
    k = max(1, int(P.shape[1] * start_frac))
    d = ((P[:, :k, L_SH] - P[:, :k, R_SH]) + (P[:, :k, L_HIP] - P[:, :k, R_HIP])).mean(axis=1)
    theta = np.arctan2(d[:, 2], d[:, 0])
    c, s = np.cos(theta)[:, None, None], np.sin(theta)[:, None, None]
    out = P.copy()
    out[..., 0] = c * P[..., 0] + s * P[..., 2]
    out[..., 2] = -s * P[..., 0] + c * P[..., 2]
    return out


def shoulder_yaw(P):
    d = (P[:, :, L_SH] - P[:, :, R_SH]).mean(axis=1)
    return np.degrees(np.arctan2(d[:, 2], d[:, 0]))


P_scaled = scale_normalize(P)
P_canon = canonicalize_rotation(P_scaled)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax, (arr, title) in zip(axes, [(P, "Raw coordinates"), (P_canon, "After rotation alignment")]):
    yaw = shoulder_yaw(arr)
    for cam, color in zip((1, 2, 3), ("tab:blue", "tab:orange", "tab:green")):
        m = (meta.cam == cam).values
        ax.scatter(meta.orientation[m] + (cam - 2) * 1.5, yaw[m], s=3, alpha=0.25, color=color, label=f"camera {cam}")
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("participant orientation (degrees)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("shoulder-line direction (degrees)")
leg = axes[0].legend(markerscale=4, fontsize=8)
for h in leg.legend_handles: h.set_alpha(1)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(FIG / "fig_p2_rotation.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
print("Spread of shoulder-line direction (std, degrees): raw %.1f, aligned %.1f"
      % (shoulder_yaw(P).std(), shoulder_yaw(P_canon).std()))

2.3 Feature sets¶

Four representations of the same repetitions:

Key Features Size per frame
raw 3D coordinates as provided 99
scaled Coordinates divided by torso length 99
aligned Scaled coordinates, rotated to a common facing direction 99
biomech Joint angles, segment tilts, and stance-width ratios, plus their velocities 44

The biomechanical set is built from quantities a clinician would look at: elbow, shoulder, hip, knee and ankle angles; trunk lean, shoulder and hip tilt, trunk twist, head tilt; whether the arm moves in the plane of the body; knee and ankle separation relative to hip width; and foot inclination.

In [4]:
def joint_angle(a, b, c):
    # Angle at b (degrees) between segments b->a and b->c.
    return vector_angle(a - b, c - b)


def vector_angle(u, v, unsigned_axis=False):
    cos = (u * v).sum(-1) / (np.linalg.norm(u, axis=-1) * np.linalg.norm(v, axis=-1) + 1e-9)
    if unsigned_axis:
        cos = np.abs(cos)
    return np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cos, -1, 1)))


def biomech_features(P):
    J = lambda i: P[:, :, i]
    mid_sh, mid_hip = (J(11) + J(12)) / 2, (J(23) + J(24)) / 2
    trunk, sh_line, hip_line = mid_sh - mid_hip, J(11) - J(12), J(23) - J(24)
    vertical = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0], dtype=P.dtype)
    hip_width = np.linalg.norm(hip_line, axis=-1) + 1e-9
    f = {
        "elbow_L": joint_angle(J(11), J(13), J(15)), "elbow_R": joint_angle(J(12), J(14), J(16)),
        "shoulder_L": joint_angle(J(23), J(11), J(13)), "shoulder_R": joint_angle(J(24), J(12), J(14)),
        "hip_L": joint_angle(J(11), J(23), J(25)), "hip_R": joint_angle(J(12), J(24), J(26)),
        "knee_L": joint_angle(J(23), J(25), J(27)), "knee_R": joint_angle(J(24), J(26), J(28)),
        "ankle_L": joint_angle(J(25), J(27), J(31)), "ankle_R": joint_angle(J(26), J(28), J(32)),
        "trunk_lean": vector_angle(trunk, vertical, unsigned_axis=True),
        "shoulder_tilt": vector_angle(sh_line, vertical),
        "hip_tilt": vector_angle(hip_line, vertical),
        "trunk_twist": vector_angle(sh_line, hip_line),
        "head_tilt": vector_angle(J(7) - J(8), sh_line),
        "neck": vector_angle(J(0) - mid_sh, trunk),
        "arm_plane_L": vector_angle(J(13) - J(11), sh_line), "arm_plane_R": vector_angle(J(14) - J(12), sh_line),
        "foot_incline_L": vector_angle(J(31) - J(29), vertical), "foot_incline_R": vector_angle(J(32) - J(30), vertical),
    }
    feats = [v / 180.0 for v in f.values()]
    names = list(f)
    feats += [np.linalg.norm(J(25) - J(26), axis=-1) / hip_width, np.linalg.norm(J(27) - J(28), axis=-1) / hip_width]
    names += ["knee_width_ratio", "ankle_width_ratio"]
    static = np.stack(feats, axis=-1)                                # (N, T, 22)
    velocity = np.gradient(static, axis=1)                           # per normalised time step
    return np.concatenate([static, velocity], axis=-1), names + [n + "_vel" for n in names]


biomech, biomech_names = biomech_features(P)
FEATURES = {
    "raw": P.reshape(N, T, -1),
    "scaled": P_scaled.reshape(N, T, -1),
    "aligned": P_canon.reshape(N, T, -1),
    "biomech": biomech.astype(np.float32),
}
FEATURE_LABEL = {"raw": "Raw 3D coordinates", "scaled": "Scaled coordinates",
                 "aligned": "Scaled + rotation-aligned coordinates", "biomech": "Biomechanical features"}
for k, v in FEATURES.items():
    assert np.isfinite(v).all()
    print(f"{k:8s} {v.shape}")


def summarize(seq):
    # Per-repetition summary statistics over time: mean, min, max, range of every feature.
    return np.concatenate([seq.mean(1), seq.min(1), seq.max(1), seq.max(1) - seq.min(1)], axis=1)

raw      (4995, 64, 99)
scaled   (4995, 64, 99)
aligned  (4995, 64, 99)
biomech  (4995, 64, 44)

2.4 Train / validation / test split¶

With five participants, a random split would put the same person (and the same repetition seen from another camera) on both sides and overstate performance. The split is therefore by participant:

  • Test: one participant is held out completely and is not touched in this notebook. It is reserved for the final evaluation.
  • Train / validation: the other four participants are used in a 4-fold leave-one-participant-out scheme. Each fold trains on three participants and validates on the fourth.

All three camera views of a repetition always stay in the same split. Reported validation metrics are the mean over the four folds, so every number is measured on people the model has not seen.

In [5]:
persons = sorted(meta.person.unique())

FOLDS = [(np.where(meta.person.isin([p for p in dev_persons if p != v]))[0], np.where(meta.person == v)[0], v)
         for v in dev_persons]

2.5 Batching¶

A small Dataset returns the features, a one-hot code for which exercise is being performed, and the label. Features are standardised with the mean and standard deviation of the training fold only. The exercise code is given to the model because the same pose can be correct for one exercise and an error for another, and the exercise is known in any real use.

In [6]:
class RepDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, x, exercise_ids, y):
        self.x = torch.as_tensor(x, dtype=torch.float32)
        self.ex = nn.functional.one_hot(torch.as_tensor([EX_INDEX[e] for e in exercise_ids]), 3).float()
        self.y = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(y), dtype=torch.float32)

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.y)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.x[i], self.ex[i], self.y[i]


def make_loaders(feature_key, kind, train_idx, val_idx, seed):
    seq = FEATURES[feature_key]
    if kind == "mlp":
        x = summarize(seq)                                           # (N, 4F)
        mu, sd = x[train_idx].mean(0), x[train_idx].std(0) + 1e-6
    else:
        x = seq                                                      # (N, T, F)
        mu, sd = x[train_idx].mean((0, 1)), x[train_idx].std((0, 1)) + 1e-6
    x = (x - mu) / sd
    if kind != "mlp":
        x = x.transpose(0, 2, 1)                                     # (N, F, T) for Conv1d
    ex, y = meta.exercise_id.values, meta.y.values
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    train = DataLoader(RepDataset(x[train_idx], ex[train_idx], y[train_idx]), batch_size=BATCH, shuffle=True, generator=g)
    val = DataLoader(RepDataset(x[val_idx], ex[val_idx], y[val_idx]), batch_size=512, shuffle=False)
    return train, val


tr_loader, va_loader = make_loaders("aligned", "cnn", FOLDS[0][0], FOLDS[0][1], seed=0)
xb, eb, yb = next(iter(tr_loader))
print("Sequence batch:", tuple(xb.shape), tuple(eb.shape), tuple(yb.shape))
xb, eb, yb = next(iter(make_loaders("aligned", "mlp", FOLDS[0][0], FOLDS[0][1], seed=0)[0]))
print("Summary batch: ", tuple(xb.shape), tuple(eb.shape), tuple(yb.shape))

3. Models¶

Baseline: MLP on summary statistics. Each repetition is reduced to the mean, minimum, maximum and range of every feature over time. The model sees how far each joint moved but not the order in which things happened.

Advanced model (first version): 1D CNN. Three convolutional blocks over the full 64-frame sequence, followed by global average and max pooling. This model can use the shape and timing of the movement.

Both are trained the same way: AdamW, binary cross-entropy, a fixed number of epochs. There is no early stopping on the validation fold, so the validation number is not used to pick the model it then evaluates.

In [7]:
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in, n_ex=3, hidden=(128, 64), dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        layers, d = [], n_in + n_ex
        for h in hidden:
            layers += [nn.Linear(d, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(dropout)]
            d = h
        self.net = nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(d, 1))

    def forward(self, x, ex):
        return self.net(torch.cat([x, ex], dim=1)).squeeze(1)


class CNN1D(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_feat, n_ex=3, widths=(64, 128, 128), kernel=5, dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        blocks, d = [], n_feat
        for i, w in enumerate(widths):
            blocks += [nn.Conv1d(d, w, kernel, padding=kernel // 2), nn.BatchNorm1d(w), nn.ReLU()]
            if i < len(widths) - 1:
                blocks.append(nn.MaxPool1d(2))
            d = w
        self.features = nn.Sequential(*blocks)
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(2 * d + n_ex, 64), nn.ReLU(),
                                  nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(64, 1))

    def forward(self, x, ex):
        h = self.features(x)
        h = torch.cat([h.mean(dim=2), h.amax(dim=2), ex], dim=1)
        return self.head(h).squeeze(1)


def build_model(kind, feature_key):
    n_feat = FEATURES[feature_key].shape[2]
    return MLP(4 * n_feat) if kind == "mlp" else CNN1D(n_feat)


for kind in ("mlp", "cnn"):
    for key in ("aligned", "biomech"):
        n = sum(p.numel() for p in build_model(kind, key).parameters())
        print(f"{kind.upper():4s} on {key:8s}: {n:,} parameters")

MLP  on aligned : 59,521 parameters
MLP  on biomech : 31,361 parameters
CNN  on aligned : 172,225 parameters
CNN  on biomech : 154,625 parameters
In [8]:
def train_model(kind, feature_key, train_idx, val_idx, seed):
    # Train one model on one fold. Returns per-epoch history and final validation probabilities.
    torch.manual_seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed)
    train_loader, val_loader = make_loaders(feature_key, kind, train_idx, val_idx, seed)
    model = build_model(kind, feature_key).to(device)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=LR, weight_decay=WEIGHT_DECAY)
    loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
    y_val = meta.y.values[val_idx]
    history = []
    for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
        model.train()
        total, count = 0.0, 0
        for x, ex, y in train_loader:
            x, ex, y = x.to(device), ex.to(device), y.to(device)
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_fn(model(x, ex), y)
            loss.backward(); opt.step()
            total += loss.item() * len(y); count += len(y)
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            logits = torch.cat([model(x.to(device), ex.to(device)) for x, ex, _ in val_loader]).cpu()
        prob = torch.sigmoid(logits).numpy()
        history.append(dict(epoch=epoch + 1, train_loss=total / count,
                            val_loss=loss_fn(logits, torch.as_tensor(y_val, dtype=torch.float32)).item(),
                            val_acc=accuracy_score(y_val, prob > 0.5)))
    return pd.DataFrame(history), prob


def run_condition(name, kind, feature_key):
    # 4 folds x 3 seeds for one (model, features) condition.
    t0 = time.time()
    scores, preds, hists = [], [], []
    for seed in SEEDS:
        for train_idx, val_idx, val_person in FOLDS:
            hist, prob = train_model(kind, feature_key, train_idx, val_idx, seed)
            y = meta.y.values[val_idx]
            scores.append(dict(condition=name, seed=seed, val_person=val_person, acc=accuracy_score(y, prob > 0.5),
                               f1=f1_score(y, prob > 0.5), auc=roc_auc_score(y, prob)))
            preds.append(meta.iloc[val_idx].assign(condition=name, seed=seed, prob=prob, pred=(prob > 0.5).astype(int)))
            hists.append(hist.assign(condition=name, seed=seed, val_person=val_person))
    scores = pd.DataFrame(scores)
    print(f"{name:34s} val acc {scores.acc.mean():.3f}  ({time.time() - t0:.0f}s)")
    return scores, pd.concat(preds), pd.concat(hists)

4. Sanity check: how much does duration give away?¶

Part 1 found that incorrect repetitions are longer on average. Before training anything, this is how well a logistic regression does using only the original length of the repetition and which exercise it is. Resampling to a fixed length removes this information from every model below, so their scores have to come from the movement itself.

In [9]:
def duration_features(idx):
    d = meta.n_frames.values[idx, None] / 100.0
    onehot = np.eye(3)[[EX_INDEX[e] for e in meta.exercise_id.values[idx]]]
    return np.concatenate([onehot, onehot * d], axis=1)

dur = []
for train_idx, val_idx, v in FOLDS:
    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(duration_features(train_idx), meta.y.values[train_idx])
    dur.append(accuracy_score(meta.y.values[val_idx], clf.predict(duration_features(val_idx))))
print("Duration-only validation accuracy: %.3f ± %.3f (chance = 0.500)" % (np.mean(dur), np.std(dur)))

Duration-only validation accuracy: 0.536 ± 0.032 (chance = 0.500)

5. Experiments¶

Eight conditions: two models on four feature sets. Reading across feature sets with the model fixed is Experiment 1; reading across models with the features fixed is Experiment 2. Every condition is trained on the same four folds with three random seeds.

In [10]:
CONDITIONS = [(f"{kind.upper()} | {key}", kind, key) for kind in ("mlp", "cnn")
              for key in ("raw", "scaled", "aligned", "biomech")]
all_scores, all_preds, all_hists = [], [], []
for name, kind, key in CONDITIONS:
    s, p, h = run_condition(name, kind, key)
    all_scores.append(s); all_preds.append(p); all_hists.append(h)
scores, preds, hists = pd.concat(all_scores), pd.concat(all_preds), pd.concat(all_hists)
ORDER = [c[0] for c in CONDITIONS]

5.1 Results¶

Validation metrics are averaged over the four held-out participants and three seeds. acc_std_folds is the spread across participants (after averaging seeds) and acc_std_seeds is the spread across seeds (after averaging participants). A difference between two conditions that is smaller than the seed spread is noise.

In [11]:
by_fold = scores.groupby(["condition", "val_person"]).acc.mean().unstack()
by_seed = scores.groupby(["condition", "seed"]).acc.mean().unstack()
results = pd.DataFrame({
    "model": [c.split(" | ")[0] for c in ORDER],
    "features": [FEATURE_LABEL[c.split(" | ")[1]] for c in ORDER],
    "val_acc": scores.groupby("condition").acc.mean().reindex(ORDER).values,
    "acc_std_folds": by_fold.std(axis=1).reindex(ORDER).values,
    "acc_std_seeds": by_seed.std(axis=1).reindex(ORDER).values,
    "val_f1": scores.groupby("condition").f1.mean().reindex(ORDER).values,
    "val_auc": scores.groupby("condition").auc.mean().reindex(ORDER).values,
}, index=ORDER)

5.3 Where the models succeed and fail¶

The same validation predictions, broken down three ways: by exercise, by viewing angle, and by error type. The viewing angle is the camera position minus the participant's orientation, so 0° is a frontal view and ±90° is a side view. The exercising arm is the right one. At positive angles it is on the side nearer the camera; at negative angles it is on the far side and partly hidden by the body (its mean visibility score falls to about 0.5 at the most negative angles).

5.4 Diagnostic: seen versus unseen participants¶

Training loss is far below validation loss in every condition. To see whether that gap comes from the models failing to learn the task or from failing to transfer to a new person, the same models are trained on a split that mixes participants: a random 25% of repetitions from the four development participants is held out (all three views of a repetition together), so the validation set contains people the model has seen. This is not a valid estimate of real performance. It is only a ceiling to compare against.

5.5 Draft of the advanced model: bidirectional GRU with attention¶

The 1D CNN is only a first step beyond the baseline. The model I intend to develop as the advanced architecture is a bidirectional GRU with attention pooling. The GRU reads the repetition forwards and backwards, and the attention layer learns which moments of the movement matter most for the decision, which should also make the model's mistakes easier to inspect.

This is a rough draft. It is run here with default settings, one seed, and two feature sets, and it is not part of the results table. Still to do: tuning, more seeds, the remaining feature sets, visibility scores as an extra input, augmentation, and looking at where the attention weights fall.

In [ ]:
class BiGRUAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_feat, n_ex=3, hidden=64, layers=2, dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        self.proj = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(n_feat, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(dropout))
        self.gru = nn.GRU(hidden, hidden, num_layers=layers, batch_first=True, bidirectional=True, dropout=dropout)
        self.attn = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * hidden, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 1))
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(2 * hidden + n_ex, 64), nn.ReLU(),
                                  nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(64, 1))

    def forward(self, x, ex, return_attention=False):
        h, _ = self.gru(self.proj(x.transpose(1, 2)))            # (N, T, 2 * hidden)
        w = torch.softmax(self.attn(h).squeeze(-1), dim=1)       # (N, T) attention over time
        pooled = (h * w.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(dim=1)
        out = self.head(torch.cat([pooled, ex], dim=1)).squeeze(1)
        return (out, w) if return_attention else out


_build_baseline_model = build_model

def build_model(kind, feature_key):
    if kind == "bigru":
        return BiGRUAttention(FEATURES[feature_key].shape[2])
    return _build_baseline_model(kind, feature_key)

6. Results table and progress summary¶

Table 1

Preliminary results: mean validation accuracy over four held-out participants and three seeds, ± the spread across participants

Model / Experiment Main change Validation accuracy Observation
Baseline MLP on summary statistics of raw 3D coordinates 0.715 ± 0.067 Well above chance (0.50) and above what repetition length alone gives (0.536), so the model is learning from the movement. The same model reaches 0.865 on participants it has seen, so most of the remaining error is failure to transfer to a new person.
Exp 1a: features Coordinates scaled by torso length 0.706 ± 0.064 No real change. Differences in body size are not what limits the baseline.
Exp 1b: features Scaled and rotated to a common facing direction 0.717 ± 0.052 No real change, even though alignment removes almost all of the orientation spread (43° to 5°). Facing direction is not the bottleneck for this model.
Exp 1c: features Biomechanical features (angles, tilts, ratios, velocities) 0.718 ± 0.058 Same overall accuracy with fewer than half the inputs. It changes which errors are caught (bent arm 0.50 to 0.73, torso to side 0.88 to 0.79) without improving the total, so the hypothesis that angles generalize better is not supported yet.
Exp 2a: model 1D CNN on raw coordinates (vs Baseline) 0.739 ± 0.075 About 2 points better, and better for all four held-out participants. Using the full sequence helps a little, consistently.
Exp 2b: model 1D CNN on scaled coordinates (vs 1a) 0.736 ± 0.083 About 3 points better on average, but worse for one of the four participants.
Exp 2c: model 1D CNN on aligned coordinates (vs 1b) 0.708 ± 0.062 No gain; the only feature set where the CNN does not help. It raises more false alarms than any other condition. I can't explain this yet.
Exp 2d: model 1D CNN on biomechanical features (vs 1c) 0.739 ± 0.066 About 2 points better for all four participants, but with the largest gap between training and validation loss (0.05 vs 1.49). This is the most overfit model.

Experiment 1 changes only the features (model fixed to the MLP). Experiment 2 changes only the model (each CNN row is compared with the MLP row that uses the same features). Seed-to-seed variation is about 0.01, and repeated runs of the CNN differ by about the same amount.

What is working¶

  • The data pipeline. Repetitions are sliced, resampled to a fixed length, converted into four feature sets, split by participant, standardized on training data only, and batched. One participant is held out as a test set and has not been touched.
  • Both models train. The MLP baseline and a first 1D CNN run on every feature set, and all eight conditions beat chance and the duration-only check by a wide margin.
  • The experiments isolate one factor each, and the per-exercise, per-view and per-error breakdowns come from the same validation predictions.

What the results say so far¶

  • Generalizing to a new person is the main problem. Accuracy is 0.71 to 0.74 on an unseen participant but 0.86 to 0.91 when the participant was seen during training. That 14 to 20 point gap is far larger than any difference between feature sets or models.
  • The mistakes are mostly false alarms. The models catch 80 to 84% of incorrect repetitions but pass only 58 to 64% of correct ones. A new person's normal way of moving is often read as an error. Arm abduction is the hardest exercise (0.60 to 0.67), where barely half of correct repetitions pass.
  • Feature representation made no measurable difference. The four feature sets are within about one point of each other under the MLP. Rotation alignment did what it was designed to do but did not help.
  • Viewpoint matters, and no feature set fixes it. Accuracy is lowest (0.63 to 0.69) when the exercising arm is on the far side of the body from the camera, where MediaPipe's confidence in that arm drops to about 0.5. Biomechanical features are no more robust here than raw coordinates.
  • The CNN is modestly better than the MLP on three of four feature sets, by 2 to 3 points.

What is not working¶

  • Overfitting. Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises in every condition. Nothing has been tuned and there is no augmentation yet.
  • Too little statistical power to rank feature sets. Accuracy varies by 5 to 8 points from one held-out participant to the next, which is larger than every difference in the table. Only the CNN versus MLP comparison on raw and biomechanical features is consistent across all four participants.
  • My hypothesis is not supported so far. I expected joint angles to transfer better across people and views than coordinates. At this stage they do not.
  • The advanced model is a rough draft. The 1D CNN is only a first step past the baseline. I have drafted a bidirectional GRU with attention as the main advanced model. An untuned, single-seed run gives 0.72 to 0.73, no better than the CNN, and it is not in the table. The CNN's poor result on aligned coordinates is also unexplained.

Next steps¶

  1. Attack the person gap directly: stronger regularization, augmentation (random rotation, scaling, time warping), and features measured relative to each repetition's own starting pose.
  2. Run the viewpoint experiment properly by training on some viewing angles and testing on others.
  3. Develop the bidirectional GRU with attention: tune it, run it on every feature set with several seeds, give it the visibility scores, and look at where its attention falls.
  4. Move to evaluation that rotates the held-out participant, so the final numbers do not depend on one person.
